steps.title: Prepare PLA reagents
steps.instruction: Make all solutions needed for the proximity ligation assay and store them under the specified conditions.

substeps.instruction: Prepare a 4 % formaldehyde fixation buffer by diluting formaldehyde in 1X DPBS; store at 4 °C for up to 1 month (prepare in a fume hood, wear gloves and mask).
Prepare a 0.3 % Triton‑X‑100 permeabilization buffer by diluting Triton‑X‑100 in 1X DPBS; store at 4 °C for up to 1 month.

Dissolve the contents of one pouch each of Duolink In Situ PLA Fluorescence Wash Buffer A and Wash Buffer B in distilled water to a final volume of 1 L; store at 4 °C for up to 1 month and do not use buffers older than one month. (Alternative recipes are listed in the Materials section.)

steps.title: Fix, permeabilize, and block cells
steps.instruction: Treat cultured cells in a 96‑well glass‑bottom plate with fixation, permeabilization, and blocking solutions before antibody incubation.

substeps.instruction: Using a vacuum pump or micropipette, aspirate the growth medium from each well and rinse the cells once with 150 µL 1X DPBS.
Add 100 µL of the 4 % formaldehyde fixation buffer to each well and incubate for 10–15 min at 20–22 °C (do not exceed 15 min).
Aspirate the fixation solution, rinse once with 150 µL 1X DPBS. (Pause point: after fixation, plates can be stored in 1X DPBS at 4 °C for up to 1 week.)
Add 100 µL of the 0.3 % Triton‑X‑100 permeabilization buffer to each well and incubate for 10 min at 20–22 °C.
Discard the permeabilization solution and rinse once with 150 µL 1X DPBS.

Add 50 µL of the blocking solution supplied with the Duolink In Situ PLA probe kit to each well and incubate in a 37 °C humidified incubator for 30 min. (Alternative: 5 % normal goat serum diluted in 1X DPBS may be used for blocking.)

steps.title: Acquire and analyze PLA images
steps.instruction: Capture fluorescence images of the PLA reaction and quantify PLA foci per nucleus using Fiji/ImageJ.

substeps.instruction: Acquire images on an LSM780 confocal microscope, save each field as a CZI file, and optionally process the raw data with Zeiss Zen Blue software.
Open the CZI files in Fiji (ImageJ) and split the channels (e.g., DAPI/Hoechst and PLA fluorescence).
Select the DAPI channel, open Image → Adjust → Threshold and set the threshold value to 25 so that each nucleus appears as a single region.
Run Analyze → Analyze Particles, set size discrimination to a minimum of 20 µm² and a maximum of ∞, then click OK; the resulting image and table give the nuclear count.
Select the PLA channel, open Process → Find Maxima, set Prominence as needed, choose ‘Single points’ as the output type, and click OK to generate a binary image with one pixel per PLA focus.

Open the ROI Manager (Analyze → Tools → ROI Manager), check ‘Show All’ to overlay the PLA‑pixel ROI on the nuclear mask, then use Measure to obtain a results table. The RawIntDen column equals 255 × (number of PLA foci); divide each RawIntDen value by 255 to obtain the number of PLA foci per nucleus.
Keep all Fiji parameter settings identical for every image to ensure comparable quantification across samples.

description: Transcription is the first step to converting genetic information from DNAs to functional products, such as proteins. One of the central players in transcription are transcription factors (TFs), which dictate gene transcription through direct binding to specific DNA sequences in the genome. To investigate the DNA binding of TFs, a variety of techniques have been developed, including Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) and Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP).3,4 Nonetheless, some limitations are associated with these widely applied techniques, including lengthy procedures, complex non-physiological manipulations, and the requirement for large amounts of samples. Importantly, these techniques can only provide information on the population mean. The protocol below describes the steps of adapting the Proximity Ligation Assay (PLA) technique to detect the DNA binding of TFs in situ at the single-cell resolution. As a recently emerged technique, PLA can detect and visualize endogenous protein-protein interactions and post-translational modifications of proteins.5,6 The success of PLA is primarily determined by the closeness of two targets of interest (within 40 nm).5,6 For typical indirect PLA, two primary antibodies raised in two different species and displaying high specificities towards the targets of interest are required. This protocol can be conveniently applied to any cultured cells and, with some modifications, may also be used on frozen or fixed tissues.
